about: Wild country as places on the ground: for each kind of country, the landmarks a stretch of it holds (where it is crossed by water, high ground, and the places people have used), the trails between them, the way in from a road or a settlement, and what it is like to be lost in it. A landmark with a view can be climbed to learn the lie of the land; one with water can be followed.

trails: a holloway between banks of root
a green ride between the trees
a carters' track, soft with leaf

entry.name: the edge of {zone} by {from}
entry.scene: Here {zone} begins: hazel and thorn at first, then oak, and the light under them goes green. {from} is behind you, out in the open.

lost.name: somewhere in {zone}
lost.scene: Somewhere in {zone}. The trees are all alike in every direction, and the light gives no hint which way is which.
lost.astray: The trees close in, and the path you were following is not there any more. You have no idea which way you have come.
lost.guided: {?m} stops, looks up at the light coming through the leaves, and turns you a quarter round. 'This way.' And it is.

landmarks.name: the charcoal-burners' clearing
landmarks.scene: A clearing where charcoal has been burned for years: rings of black earth, a turf hut with its door off, cordwood stacked under bark. The smell of old smoke hangs over all of it.
landmarks.ambience: A woodpecker is at work somewhere close.

things.name: the turf hut
things.seen: The turf hut's door lies in the nettles beside it.
things.closer: Inside, the hut is dry and smells of smoke: a bed of bracken, and a crock with a broken lip.

find.name: a pine-knot torch
find.seen: Stuck in the turf over the doorway is a pine-knot torch, pitched and ready, as burners leave one for whoever comes after.

things.name: the burning-rings
things.seen: The burning-rings lie black in the grass.
things.closer: Each ring is a shallow hollow of fine black earth, raked clean. The newest still has lumps of charcoal at its rim that the rake missed.
things.known: Some of the rings lie under moss a hand deep, and some are bare: charcoal has been burned here a ring at a time for longer than the oldest of these trees has stood.

landmarks.name: the great oak
landmarks.scene: An oak stands in a clearing of its own, too broad for three people to circle with their arms. Its lowest limbs would roof a cart, and the bark is worn smooth where climbers have gone up.
landmarks.ambience: Jays scold from somewhere in the crown.

things.name: the hollow in the oak
things.seen: A hollow opens in the oak's trunk at the height of your head.
things.closer: The hollow has been used as a cupboard: a flat stone keeps its floor dry.

find.name: a stub of candle
find.seen: On the stone lies a twist of oilcloth with a stub of candle in it.

things.known: Cut into the lip of the hollow and worn nearly smooth: three strokes and a ring. It is a drovers' sign, and an old one, for a place where word can be left for whoever comes after.

landmarks.name: the spring under the beeches
landmarks.scene: Water comes out of a mossy bank under old beeches and runs away in a channel lined with stones. Someone set those stones; someone hung the rag on the branch above.
landmarks.ambience: A wren goes in and out of the bank by the water.

things.name: the rags on the branch
things.seen: Rags hang from a beech branch over the water.
things.closer: Not one rag but dozens, tied one over another along the branch: the oldest rotted to threads, the newest still bright where the knot hides it.
things.known: It is a rag-well. A strip of a sick person's clothing is tied over the water, and as the cloth wastes away, so does the sickness. The bright one was tied this season.

do.name: Tie a strip of cloth on the branch
do.done: Your strip of cloth hangs over the water with the others.

things.name: the stones of the channel
things.seen: Dressed stones line the channel away from the spring.
things.closer: The channel stones are cut square, not gathered, and the one at the spring's mouth has letters on it, half under the water.
things.known: The letters are old and plain, and the water has nearly worn them away: a name, and after it, MADE THIS FOR ALL WHO PASS.

landmarks.name: the holly hollow
landmarks.scene: A hollow full of holly, dark even at noon, the ground dry underneath and littered with prickled leaves. A good place to keep out of the rain, and to keep out of sight.
landmarks.ambience: Something small rustles away under the holly.

things.name: the dry ground under the holly
things.seen: Under the holly the ground is dry as a floor.
things.closer: Somebody has slept here, though not lately: a hollow scraped in the leaf-litter, and a ring of stones round old ash, kept small so that the smoke would not show.
things.known: Whoever slept here knew the wood. The fire was lit where the holly would break up the smoke, and they left by the stream, where a track does not keep.

landmarks.name: the old bank
landmarks.scene: A long bank and ditch run through the wood, grown over with trees as old as any around them. Somebody dug it to mark something, long before anyone now living.
landmarks.ambience: A badger's path runs along the top of the bank.

things.name: the ditch under the bank
things.seen: A ditch full of leaves runs along the foot of the bank.
things.closer: Where a badger has dug into the bank, the spoil is full of more than earth: sherds of black pot, and a pin of bone.
things.known: The pot is the old people's, of the kind found in barrows. The bank is older than the wood: it marked the edge of somebody's land when all this was open country.

landmarks.name: the windfall
landmarks.scene: A storm has had a row of beeches down: they lie where they fell, roots in the air, and the light comes in where they stood. Bramble has already taken the gap.
landmarks.ambience: Bees are busy in the bramble.

things.name: the root-plate of the fallen beech
things.seen: The roots of the biggest beech stand up higher than a door.
things.closer: In the pit the roots tore open, a yard down, is something pale: the worked edge of a stone trough, never meant to be seen again.
things.known: The trough's lip is worn in two places by ropes. It was the head of a well once, and there was a steading here before there was a wood.

landmarks.name: the pollards
landmarks.scene: Ancient pollarded oaks stand about a glade, each one hollow, each with a crown of straight poles cut and grown again for longer than the wood has had its name.
landmarks.ambience: An owl sits in one of the hollows, and does not move.

things.name: the cut crowns
things.seen: Every pollard's crown is a bundle of straight poles.
things.closer: The poles were all cut at the height of a man standing on a cart, the last time not many years ago. In one hollow, out of the weather, a billhook hangs on a peg.
things.known: Pollards are cut every dozen years or so, for poles and for fodder. This wood looks wild, but somebody still works it, and will be back when the poles are grown.

water.name: the ford over the {river}
water.scene: The {river} comes through the wood here over gravel and is shallow enough to wade. Deer have trodden the banks to mud.
water.ambience: A kingfisher goes downstream like a thrown stone.

things.name: the gravel bar
things.seen: A bar of gravel runs out into the {river} below the ford.
things.closer: The water has sorted the gravel into bands, coarse to fine, and in the finest something glints: a brass button, green at the edges, with a badge on it.
things.known: The badge is a pair of crossed keys, a reeve's livery, from when this ford was on a road and somebody took a toll at it.

water.name: the footbridge over the {river}
water.scene: A single split trunk lies across the {river} where the banks are steep, with a rail of one pole. The water underneath is deep and brown.
water.ambience: Trout hang in the shadow of the bridge.

things.name: the bridge's rail
things.seen: The rail of the footbridge is a single pole lashed on with withies.
things.closer: The trunk was split with wedges and adzed flat on top. The rail-pole is newer, lashed with fresh withies: someone keeps this bridge.
things.known: The withies were cut this spring, from the willows a little upstream. Whoever mends the bridge comes this way every year.

view.change: Climb up and look out over {zone}
view.seen: From up there the wood is a roof of green, and you can see where everything lies: the clearings, the line of the water, the road beyond the trees.
view.unseen: The lowest limb is within reach.

entry.name: the edge of {zone} by {from}
entry.scene: Where the fields end, {zone} begins: black water between tussocks, reed higher than your head, and the smell of it. {from} is behind you, on the firm ground.

lost.name: somewhere in {zone}
lost.scene: Somewhere out in {zone}. Reed on every side, higher than your head, and water between. Every channel looks like the last.
lost.astray: The stakes give out, and the reed closes behind you. You cannot see the firm ground in any direction, nor tell which way it lies.
lost.guided: {?m} tests the ground ahead with a pole, frowns, and tries again a yard over. 'Here. Step where I step.' You come out where you meant to.

landmarks.name: the eel-catcher's hut
landmarks.scene: A hut of reed and black timber stands on stilts over the water, with eel-traps of woven willow stacked on its platform. The ladder is pulled up.
landmarks.ambience: Something slides off the bank into the water.

things.name: the eel-traps
things.seen: Eel-traps of woven willow are stacked on the hut's platform.
things.closer: The traps are long baskets with a throat that lets an eel in and not out. Two are new-woven and still green, and cords from the platform run down into the water.
things.known: Traps are set at dusk and lifted at dawn, and these are set: whoever owns the hut will be back for them in the morning.

landmarks.name: the duck decoy
landmarks.scene: A pool with curving arms of netting going off it into the reed: a decoy for ducks, the screens of reed still standing, the nets rotted in the water.
landmarks.ambience: Duck get up off the pool all at once with a noise like applause.

things.name: the reed screens
things.seen: Reed screens stand along the decoy's curving arms.
things.closer: The screens are set so that someone walking behind them cannot be seen from the pool. There is a peep-hole cut in each, and at the end a little trap-door for a dog.
things.known: The ducks follow a dog they take for a fox, up the netted arm, until they cannot turn: that is how a decoy is worked. This one has not been worked for years, and the ducks have forgotten.

landmarks.name: the alder island
landmarks.scene: A low island of firm ground stands up out of the fen, crowded with alders and one tall willow. From its top you could see over the reed.
landmarks.ambience: A heron stands at the island's edge and does not trouble to move.

things.name: the dug-out boat
things.seen: A dug-out boat lies upside down under the alders.
things.closer: The boat is a single oak trunk, hollowed by fire and adze, black with age and still sound. Its paddle lies underneath, and its bow is carved into a beast's head, worn nearly smooth.
things.known: A beast's head on the bow was the fen-folk's way before the drainers came. A boat like this is a hundred years old if it is a day, and somebody has kept it sound.

landmarks.name: the mere
landmarks.scene: Open water: a mere ringed with reed, so still it holds the sky. Old stakes stand in a line out into it and stop, as if a path had once gone further.
landmarks.ambience: A grebe dives and comes up a long way off.

things.name: the line of stakes
things.seen: Old stakes stand in a line out into the mere.
things.closer: The stakes are black oak, sharpened at the top. Where the line stops you can see, under the surface, a sunken causeway going on toward the middle.
things.known: A causeway out to the middle of a mere goes to something: a hold on an island long since sunk, or a place where things were given to the water. The old fen-folk did both.

landmarks.name: the broken sluice
landmarks.scene: A sluice of squared timbers stands half in the water, its gate gone, a channel running straight as a rule away from it into the reed. Somebody drained this fen once, or meant to.
landmarks.ambience: Water talks in the broken gate.

things.name: the sluice-post
things.seen: The sluice-post is cut all over with marks.
things.closer: At every height the water has reached, somebody has cut a line in the post with a year beside it. The highest mark is above your head.
things.known: The years go back two hundred winters, and the highest marks are the oldest of all. The fen is drier than it was, though nobody finished draining it.

landmarks.name: the reed staithe
landmarks.scene: A landing of piled faggots where the reed-cutters bring their bundles out. Cut reed is stacked here in ricks, waiting for a boat.
landmarks.ambience: Reed-buntings sit on the ricks.

things.name: the reed ricks
things.seen: Ricks of cut reed stand on the staithe.
things.closer: The reed is tied in bundles a fathom round, the way thatchers buy it. Chalked on the end of the nearest rick is a tally, and a mark like a bird's foot.

water.name: the ford of the {river}
water.scene: The {river} spreads out slow and brown through the fen, and a line of stones lets you cross it, if you are careful where you put your feet.

things.name: the crossing-stones
things.seen: A line of stones crosses the {river}.
things.closer: One stone in the middle rocks under a foot. Somebody has set a white pebble on the stone after it, as a warning to the next to cross.

water.name: the punt-crossing of the {river}
water.scene: A flat-bottomed punt is tied to a post on this bank of the {river}, with a rope running across to the far side to pull it by.
water.ambience: The rope creaks as the current leans on the punt.

things.name: the fare-box
things.seen: A wooden box is nailed to the punt's post.
things.closer: The box has a slot in its lid and a few coppers in the bottom: the fare, left on trust for whoever keeps the punt.

view.change: Climb the willow and look out over {zone}
view.seen: From the willow you can see over the reed: the channels, the open water, the line of firm ground, and which way it all goes.
view.unseen: The willow's lowest fork is shoulder-high.

entry.name: the foot of {zone} by {from}
entry.scene: The fields give way to heather and gorse, and the land rises to the moor. {from} is behind you and below.

lost.name: somewhere on {zone}
lost.scene: Somewhere on {zone}. Heather in every direction, the same low hummocks, and a sky with no sun in it to steer by.
lost.astray: The trod you were following thins to nothing in the heather. Every rise looks like the last, and the mist has the far ones.
lost.guided: {?m} kneels to see which way the heather lies, then stands and points. 'That way.' It is.

landmarks.name: the cairn
landmarks.scene: A cairn of grey stones stands on the highest ground, taller than a man, every traveller's stone added to it. You can see a long way from here.
landmarks.ambience: A curlew calls, a long way off.

things.name: the stones of the cairn
things.seen: The cairn is built of every kind of stone the moor has.
things.closer: Every kind the moor has, and some it hasn't: a lump of white quartz, a piece of red brick, a sea-pebble a long way from any sea.
things.known: The custom is old: every traveller adds a stone for luck on the way, and so the cairn grows. The sea-pebble came farther than anyone walks now.

do.name: Add a stone of your own to the cairn
do.done: Your stone is on the cairn now, with everyone else's.

landmarks.name: the leaning stone
landmarks.scene: A single standing stone, taller than a rider, leans out of the heather as if it were listening. The ground at its foot is bare, as though something walks round it.
landmarks.ambience: Wind hums on the edge of the stone.

things.name: the bare ring round the stone
things.seen: The heather is worn away in a ring round the stone's foot.
things.closer: The ring is a path, beaten by feet going round and round, sunwise. Sheep do not walk sunwise. At the foot of the stone is a hole, worn smooth, with something in it.
things.known: People walk three times sunwise round a stone like this to ask it something, and leave the asking in the hole at its foot. What is in it now is a lock of hair, tied with thread.

do.name: Walk three times round the stone, sunwise
do.done: You have walked three times round the stone, sunwise. Nothing that you can see has changed.

landmarks.name: the shepherds' bothy
landmarks.scene: A bothy of piled stone and turf, roofed with heather, with a fold for sheep against its back wall. The ashes in its hearth are not very old.
landmarks.ambience: A wheatear flits from the wall to the fold and back.

things.name: the bothy hearth
things.seen: Ashes not long cold lie in the bothy's hearth.
things.closer: Kindling is stacked dry under the hearth-stone, as shepherds leave it for the next one caught out on the moor.

find.name: a twist of dried herbs
find.seen: In a niche in the wall is a twist of dried herbs, left the same way.

landmarks.name: the peat cuttings
landmarks.scene: The moor has been cut away in long black steps, and the peats stand drying in little stacks of three, row after row. Water lies in the bottom of the cuttings.
landmarks.ambience: Bog-cotton nods along the edge of the cuttings.

things.name: the cut face of the peat
things.seen: The cut face of the peat stands black and wet.
things.closer: In the cut face, a spade's depth down, runs a line of grey: wood, a birch branch as fresh as the day it fell, though there is no tree within a mile.
things.known: Peat keeps whatever falls into it. This moor was a birchwood once, before the peat grew over it, and that branch has lain in the dark ever since.

landmarks.name: the dewpond
landmarks.scene: A round pond lined with clay lies in a hollow of the moor, with no stream to fill it. The sheep come to it from miles, and the mud round it is printed all over.
landmarks.ambience: Skylarks go up and up over the pond.

things.name: the pond's clay lining
things.seen: Where the sheep have trodden the pond's edge, its lining shows.
things.closer: Under the trodden edge: puddled clay over a bed of straw over chalk, laid as fine as a floor. No stream fills this pond; it was made to hold the dew and the rain.
things.known: Dewpond-makers kept their craft in families and walked the moors making ponds for whoever would pay. One of them made this one, and it has held longer than the bothy has stood.

water.name: the ford of the {river}
water.scene: The {river} runs brown off the peat between banks of heather, shallow over flat stones.
water.ambience: A dipper bobs on a stone in the stream.

things.name: the flat stones of the ford
things.seen: Flat stones pave the bed of the {river} at the ford.
things.closer: The stones are laid, not lying: a pavement under the water, wide enough for a cart, the edges worn round by a long time of wheels.
things.known: A paved ford on the open moor means a road once ran here that is a sheep-trod now: the drove road that went over the tops before the valley road was made.

view.change: Climb the cairn and look out over {zone}
view.seen: From the top of the cairn the moor lies open all round: the trods, the streams, the far edge where the fields begin.
view.unseen: The stones of the cairn make a rough stair.

entry.name: the foot of {zone} by {from}
entry.scene: The ground steepens. Walls run up the fellside and give out where the bracken begins. {from} is behind you, in the valley.

lost.name: somewhere on {zone}
lost.scene: Somewhere on {zone}. Rock and scree and cloud, and the ground falling away on more sides than one.
lost.astray: The cloud comes down, and with it the end of the path. Every way you turn the ground falls away into grey.
lost.guided: {?m} watches the cloud a while, picks out a wall running down the fellside, and follows it. It brings you where you meant to go.

landmarks.name: the tarn
landmarks.scene: A tarn lies in a hollow under a crag, so dark it looks bottomless, with a little beach of grey gravel at one end. The wind falls silent here.
landmarks.ambience: A raven croaks from the crag above.

things.name: the gravel beach
things.seen: A little beach of grey gravel lies at the tarn's end.
things.closer: At the water's edge the gravel is mixed with chips of a greenish stone, flaked and sharp. Somebody sat here once and worked blades.
things.known: It is axe-stone, the green stone of the high fells, worked here and carried down to the valleys in the time before bronze.

landmarks.name: the sheepfold
landmarks.scene: A round fold of dry-stone walling stands on a shelf of the fell, its gate a hurdle tied with twine. Sheep have been in it lately.
landmarks.ambience: Sheep on the slope above stop chewing to look at you.

things.name: the hurdle gate
things.seen: The fold's gate is a hurdle tied with twine.
things.closer: The twine is new. The shepherd's mark is on the gatepost in red, a bar and a ring, and the hurdle has been patched with hazel this year.
things.known: The droppings in the fold are a day or two old: the shepherd brought the flock in to sort it, and will bring it in again before the weather turns.

landmarks.name: the crag
landmarks.scene: A crag stands out of the fellside like a broken tooth, with a ledge you could stand on and a long fall below it. From the top you would see the whole valley.
landmarks.ambience: Ravens tumble in the wind under the crag.

things.name: the ledge
things.seen: A ledge runs out along the face of the crag.
things.closer: On the ledge, out of the wind, is a ravens' nest of sticks and wool, and in the wool a scrap of red cloth and the bowl of a clay pipe.
things.known: Ravens take whatever catches their eye. The cloth and the pipe came up from the valley, a long way, in a beak.

landmarks.name: the shieling
landmarks.scene: Two huts of stone and turf stand by a beck on a green shelf of the fell, where cattle are brought up in summer. One still has its roof.
landmarks.ambience: The beck chatters past the huts.

things.name: the kist in the roofed hut
things.seen: In the roofed hut stands a kist with a lid of turf.
things.closer: In the hut are a stone bench, a cheese-press of two flat stones, and the kist, empty but for a horn spoon.

find.name: a coil of rope
find.seen: Coiled in the bottom of the kist is a rope, left there over the winter.

landmarks.name: the col
landmarks.scene: A saddle of bare ground between two summits, where the wind comes through hard and the ground is worn to the rock. A cairn marks the way down either side.
landmarks.ambience: The wind never stops.

things.name: the cairns of the way down
things.seen: A cairn marks the way down either side of the col.
things.closer: Each cairn has a long flat stone on top, pointing down its own side of the col: what a traveller caught in cloud would need, set by somebody who had been.
things.known: The pointing stones are an old kindness of the fells: follow the cairns down and you will come out where people are, whatever the cloud does.

water.name: the stepping-stones over the {river}
water.scene: The {river} comes down off the fell here in a white rush, and someone has set stepping-stones across where it runs widest.

things.name: the stepping-stones
things.seen: The stepping-stones stand square in the white water.
things.closer: They are not the fell's own stone: they are dressed blocks, square, each with a groove along it where something once ran.
things.known: Grooved for a door or a sluice-gate, they came from a building and were carried up here to be stepped on. Something stood in this valley once that was pulled down for its stone.

view.change: Climb the crag and look out over {zone}
view.seen: From the top of the crag the whole of {zone} is laid out: the paths, the becks, the folds, and the valley road below.
view.unseen: A crack runs up the crag that a careful climber could use.
